idiom_name: std::unique_ptr / std::shared_ptr / std::weak_ptr (make_unique / make_shared, custom deleters)
implementation_notes: C++ is the pattern's home: since C++11 the standard library ships the realizations, and a raw pointer in an interface documents a non-owning relationship. std::unique_ptr is move-only, so ownership transfer is compiled in and a copy is an error; std::shared_ptr keeps a control block with strong and weak counts and destroys the object through its deleter when the last strong owner goes; std::weak_ptr observes without owning and must be promoted with lock() before use. Create shared objects with std::make_shared (one allocation, exception-safe) and unique ones with std::make_unique; custom deleters adapt foreign resources (FILE*, dlopen handles) to the same discipline.
pitfalls: Two shared_ptrs constructed from the same raw pointer get two control blocks and double-delete; always adopt through make_shared/unique_ptr or enable_shared_from_this.
shared_ptr cycles leak; designate one direction weak_ptr.
Passing shared_ptr by value adds atomic refcount traffic - pass const& or a raw reference when only observing.
unique_ptr<T> with an incomplete T in a header requires the deleter to see the complete type: declare the destructor out of line.
Dereferencing a weak_ptr's lock() result outside its guard re-creates a dangling access.

variants.name: Pre-C++11 hand-written handle/body smart pointer (auto_ptr era)
variants.idiom_name: rule-of-three handle class with operator-> / operator* delegation (More C++ Idioms) plus boost::scoped_ptr / std::auto_ptr
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++11 the pattern was the whole class: a Handle wrapping Body* with overloaded operator-> and operator* for delegation (completely or less pointer-like semantics, as the More C++ Idioms entry describes), and a hand-written copy constructor, assignment operator and destructor (rule of three) to define whether copying shares, clones or transfers. std::auto_ptr is the standard library's own pre-C++11 attempt (strict ownership transfer; deprecated in C++11, removed in C++17) and boost::scoped_ptr/shared_ptr the widely used alternative; without move semantics, transfer is emulated by swap or by pass-by-value. Choose this shape only for toolchains that cannot use C++11, and then prefer boost to hand-written handles.
pitfalls: A hand-written copy/assignment that shallow-copies body_ double-deletes; honour the rule of three or delete the copy operations.
std::auto_ptr moves on copy, which is what got it removed from C++17 - do not use it in modern code.
Without move semantics, transfer goes through swap or pass-by-value and is easy to get wrong under exceptions; container behaviour depends entirely on the documented copy policy.
A templated handle in a header needs the complete body type to delete it, so pimpl separation requires out-of-line destruction.

variants.name: C++23 out_ptr/inout_ptr adapters for foreign pointer setters
variants.implementation_notes: When a foreign API hands back a raw pointer through an out-parameter (C libraries, COM, platform APIs), std::out_ptr and std::inout_ptr adapt an existing smart pointer so the smart pointer receives the new value while keeping its deleter contract and resetting safely. This replaces the pattern's weakest step - the manual 'adopt the raw pointer into a smart pointer after the call' - which leaks whenever the setter succeeds only partially or the caller forgets the adoption. The ownership model underneath is unchanged (unique_ptr/shared_ptr); the variant is distinct because it changes the interop surface. Use it in C++23 code bases that must pass smart pointers to C-style setters.
pitfalls: out_ptr-based adoption only works if the smart pointer actually receives the raw pointer; a setter that fails after writing must not leave the value adopted twice.
The deleter must match the foreign release function (fclose for FILE*, a library-specific close for its own handles); a default_delete on a foreign pointer is a mismatched free.
inout_ptr reads the current pointer before the call, so it belongs only with APIs that genuinely take a live handle in and out; mixing the adapters leaks or double-releases the old value.
The C++23 library types out_ptr_t/inout_ptr_t are required; on older standard libraries the manual adopt-after-call pattern remains, with its error-path leak risk.
